summary: Explains how to match the strengths of public keys, symmetric keys, and the overall system when public key cryptography is used to exchange symmetric keys. A system is only as strong as its weakest link, so the sizes must be chosen consistently. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: A strong lock on a weak door does not help. This explains how to choose sizes of different keys so none is the weak spot.

subtitle: How big must a public key be so it is not the weak link protecting a symmetric key?

tldr.problem: When public key cryptography is used to exchange a symmetric key, an attacker can go after either the symmetric key or the public key, so the weaker of the two sets the real security of the system.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC picks a target attack resistance in bits, then estimates how large an RSA or Diffie-Hellman modulus is needed to cost an attacker about as much as brute-forcing a symmetric key of that size, using the number field sieve as the model.
tldr.outcome: It gives a table that matches system strength, symmetric key size, RSA or DH modulus size and DSA subgroup size, and warns that the numbers are estimates, not definitive facts.

today: RFC 3766 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 86), published April 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its figures reflect the hardware and mathematics of 2004 and the RFC itself says they are estimates.

sections.title: Two Locks, One Weak Point
sections.content:
RFC 3766 starts with a house analogy. A strong lock guards the front door, and a small lockbox next to it holds the door key. A burglar will attack whichever lock is weaker, so the lockbox must be at least as strong as the door.

Key exchange has the same shape. If a message is encrypted with a symmetric key that was exchanged using public key cryptography, an attacker can either guess the symmetric key by brute force or work out the private key used for the exchange. A smart attacker works on the easier problem. Simply making the public key very long is not a good answer, because key exchanges get much more expensive in processing time as the keys grow.

The RFC gives a selection procedure: estimate the number of operations an attacker must perform and take the base-2 logarithm, called n; choose a symmetric cipher with a key of at least n bits; choose a key exchange algorithm that resists attack to at least n bits; and choose an authentication algorithm (such as an RSA or DSA signature) with the same resistance. A 1996 report recommended 90 bits as a good all-around choice, to be increased by about 2/3 bit per year, or about 96 bits in 2005.
sections.eli5: Imagine a strong front door lock with the door key hidden in a flimsy box. A burglar just breaks the box. So every lock has to be about equally hard to break.

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman and RSA Key Exchange
sections.content:
In Diffie-Hellman, Alice and Bob agree on a prime p and a generator g (often simply 2). Alice picks a secret random integer a and sends g^a mod p; Bob picks b and sends g^b mod p. Each side raises what it received to its own secret, both get the same number, and a simple function of it becomes the symmetric key k. The same idea works over elliptic curve groups, which the RFC calls a particularly efficient way to do the exchange.

In RSA key exchange, Bob has a public modulus m = p*q built from two secret primes, plus an encryption exponent e and a decryption exponent d. Alice sends k^e mod m, and Bob recovers k by computing E^d mod m. The encryption exponent can be small (for example 17 bits), but the decryption exponent has as many bits as the modulus.
sections.eli5: Two friends can each mix a secret color into a shared paint and end up with the same final color, without ever telling each other their secret. That shared color becomes their secret key.

sections.title: How Hard It Is to Break the Public Key
sections.content:
Neither RSA nor Diffie-Hellman can be broken by simple guessing: an RSA modulus has at least 512 bits, and DH exponents have at least twice as many bits as the symmetric keys derived from them. The danger is mathematical. Factoring an RSA modulus compromises the private key completely, and solving the discrete logarithm problem for a DH modulus destroys all key exchanges using it. The RFC treats the two as comparable in difficulty, with discrete logs at least 20 and possibly as much as 64 times harder.

The best known method is the number field sieve (NFS). Its cost is modeled by L(n) = k * e^((1.92 + o(1)) * cubrt(ln(n) * (ln(ln(n)))^2)). Using factoring results for RSA130, RSA140, RSA155 and RSA160 (430 to 528 bits), the authors fit k at about 0.02, which means the effective strength is about 5 or 6 bits lower than the naive formula suggests. They treat the formula as a close upper bound for the 100 to 200 decimal digit range.

Diffie-Hellman has a second attack, Pollard's rho, which finds collisions in a large number space. Because of it, to derive a key of K bits an implementation must use an exponent of at least 2*K bits. Elliptic curve versions are immune to NFS but not to this collision method.

The RFC also discusses practical limits. Robert Silverman argued that 1024-bit RSA moduli would not be factored until about 2037 because of the machines and memory needed, but the authors say the theory-based lengths are what they use. They note that a special-purpose sieving machine design called TWIRL (August 2003) might sieve a 512-bit number in 10 minutes for about $10K of hardware, and a 1024-bit number in one year for about $10M, which makes the security of 1024-bit RSA doubtful.
sections.eli5: Nobody can open this lock by trying every combination, but a clever mathematician might find a shortcut. The RFC measures how much work the best known shortcut would take and uses that to pick a lock size.

sections.title: The Cost of Bigger Keys
sections.content:
Longer keys are safer but slower, so the RFC measures the compute time. For Diffie-Hellman, doubling the size of the modular exponentiation group quadruples the number of operations. Elliptic curve groups follow the same scaling, but for equal security they use smaller numbers: a rough estimate is that an EC group with about 200 bits matches a 2048-bit modulus, and with an assumed 20 times higher cost per operation the elliptic curve version comes out about five times as fast.

For RSA with a small encryption exponent, encryption takes roughly 28 n-by-n-word multiplies, while decryption (using the Chinese Remainder Theorem) takes about j/4 of them for a j-bit modulus. Doubling the RSA modulus size makes encryption 4 times slower and decryption 8 times slower.

The RFC adds informal real-world timings, flagged as rough examples and not benchmarks. For instance, a 1024-bit modular exponentiation took 0.9 ms on a 500 MHz Itanium, and a Celeron 400 MHz took 32 msec for a 1024-bit modulus with an exponent of about 160 bits.
sections.eli5: A bigger padlock is harder to pick but also slower to open every time. Doubling the size makes the work much bigger, not just twice as big.

sections.title: Matching Public Key Size to Symmetric Key Size
sections.content:
To make the comparison concrete, the RFC assumes a system requirement of 112 bits, the upper bound for TripleDES, and states this is for illustration only and not a recommendation. It prices an attack using the 1998 EFF DES-cracking machine (US$130,000, about 1e11 DES keys per second) and then imagines an attacker with US$1 trillion. Exhausting the 2^112 TripleDES keys would take about 33 million years.

To give a public key the same resistance, the RFC solves the NFS formula for the modulus size. Against special purpose brute force hardware, the answer is a modulus of about 2100 bits. Against a conventional CPU attack it is about 2400 bits. The RFC adds that some authors, assuming NFS keeps improving, recommend over 4000 bits for protecting a 112-bit key for 50 years, which shows how hard long-term predictions are.

A one-year attack by the same trillionaire corresponds to 80 bits of strength, and a modulus of about 1200 bits is enough to protect an 80-bit key against it. For AES, the 128-bit version is treated as at least 16 bits stronger than TripleDES, so the recommended key exchange modulus is about 700 bits longer.
sections.eli5: To decide how big the lockbox needs to be, the RFC asks how much money and time a super-rich burglar would need for each lock, and then makes both locks cost about the same.

sections.title: Deriving Keys and Using Real Randomness
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman produces a secret that is hundreds or thousands of bits long, but a cipher needs far fewer. A cryptographic one-way hash function can distill it, as long as each block of the symmetric key depends on the whole DH secret, reveals nothing about it, and is not correlated with other bits. Any good hash function meets these three requirements.

If the key is longer than the hash output, the hash can be iterated. For a 192-bit key with 192 bits of strength, the RFC shows SHA(0x00 | DHkey) for bits 1-160 and a 32-bit selection of SHA(0x01 | DHkey) for bits 161-192, so the DH key feeds each part and no entropy is lost. Hashes with longer output, such as SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, can be used with the same level of security.

Finally, the secret DH exponents must be chosen from n truly random bits, where n is the system security requirement. The RFC says many security applications have been significantly weakened by insufficient random inputs.
sections.eli5: The big shared secret is like a huge pile of sand, but you only need a small cup. You scoop it in a way that depends on the whole pile. And the starting secret has to be picked truly at random, like rolling dice, not by habit.

sections.title: The Size Table
sections.content:
The conclusion is a table that assumes attackers use general purpose computers, hardware bought in the year 2000, and unchanged mathematical knowledge. For each system requirement it lists the symmetric key size, the RSA or DH modulus size and the DSA subgroup size. The DSA modulus must be as long as the DH modulus, but the size of the q subgroup also matters.

A correction follows for the TWIRL machine. If TWIRL becomes real and row reduction gets better parallelism, conservative estimates subtract about 11 bits from the system security column, so getting 89 bits of security would need an RSA modulus of about 1900 bits.
sections.eli5: The table is a cheat sheet: pick how strong you want to be, and read across to find how big each key should be.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC is frank about its limits. The equations and values are meant to be as accurate as possible for general purpose computers at the time of writing, but no prediction can be completely accurate and the formulas are not definitive statements of fact about cryptographic strength. Some of the empirical results used to calibrate them are probably not completely accurate, and that affects the estimates.
sections.eli5: These are careful guesses, not promises. Treat them like a weather forecast.

items.title: 1. Pick n
items.text: Estimate the minimum operations an attacker needs and take log base 2.

items.title: 2. Symmetric cipher
items.text: Choose a cipher with a key of at least n bits.

items.title: 3. Key exchange
items.text: Choose a key exchange resisting attack to at least n bits.

items.title: 4. Authentication
items.text: Choose an authentication algorithm with at least n bits of resistance.
